title: Old Testament Law and Islamic Sharia: Surprising Similarities
summary: How the Old Testament's legal material and Islamic Sharia actually resemble each other far more than either resembles most of the New Testament — a useful bridge point for reverts.

body.text: A comparison most Christians haven't considered

Christians raised primarily on the New Testament's teaching often find Islamic Sharia's detailed legal structure — covering diet, ritual purity, family law, and daily conduct — unfamiliar or even alien. But the Old Testament, which most Christians also consider scripture, contains an extensive legal code (particularly in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Exodus) that resembles Sharia's structure and concerns far more closely than the New Testament does.

Dietary laws (kosher rules resembling halal categories, including a shared prohibition on pork), ritual purity requirements before worship, detailed family and inheritance law, modesty requirements, and even specific corporal and capital punishments for certain offenses all appear in the Torah/Old Testament in forms structurally similar to their Islamic counterparts. A reader familiar with Leviticus would recognise the general shape and concerns of Islamic fiqh literature far more readily than a reader coming from the Sermon on the Mount alone.
Why Christianity moved away from this model

Mainstream Christian theology holds that much of the Old Testament's ceremonial and civil law was fulfilled or superseded through Christ, a theological move without an Islamic parallel — Islam does not hold that Muhammad's coming set aside the category of divine law itself, only that it delivered God's final, complete version of it. This is the real, underlying structural reason the two faiths look so different day to day despite sharing so much legal-material ancestry in the Old Testament specifically.
A genuinely useful bridge point for conversations

This comparison can help a Christian family member understand that structured religious law isn't a foreign, exclusively Islamic concept — it's present throughout scripture they already consider authoritative, in the Old Testament. Framing Sharia as "detailed divine law of the kind found throughout the Torah, continued and completed rather than newly invented" tends to land better than leaving Sharia looking like an unprecedented imposition.

body.question: Does this mean Islamic law is basically the same as Old Testament law?
body.answer: Not identical — there are real differences in specifics, sources, and later legal development in both traditions — but the structural resemblance (detailed, God-given legal codes covering ritual, diet, and daily conduct together) is genuine and worth naming, especially since it's a resemblance most Christians haven't been prompted to notice.

body.question: Why do modern Christians generally not follow Old Testament law, then?
body.answer: This is itself a genuinely debated question within Christian theology, with different traditions drawing the line differently between moral law (still binding), ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ), and civil law (tied to ancient Israel's specific context) — worth knowing exists as an internal Christian debate, not a settled, universally agreed Christian position.
